Title: Rock crystal shines a light on ancient trade
NewsSubTitle: Mayotte 2015: excavation led by Dr Stephane Pradines unearthed a treasure trove of discoveries
NewsSummary: An excavation led by ISMC Associate Professor, Dr Stephane Pradines has unearthed a treasure trove of discoveries.
NewsContent:
An excavation led by ISMC's Dr Stephane Pradines has unearthed a treasure trove of discoveries. The dig on the tiny island of Mayotte, part of the Comoros archipelagos in the Western Indian Ocean, is held every year with the aim of understanding settlement patterns and discovering more about the people who lived and traded in this part of the world.

This year, the team found large quantities of rock crystal fragments, chips and flakes of different sizes. Objects made from rock crystal are highly prized by collectors and art-lovers and are displayed worldwide in museums including the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, the Louvre in Paris and the Metropolitan Museum in New York. Indeed rock crystal is incorporated into the treasures of Christian kingdoms such as Saint Mark's Basilica in Venice and the Basilica Cathedral of Saint-Denis near Paris. 

The Mayotte site is world-renowned for its rich history and this discovery has far reaching implications for accurately pinpointing trade routes and settlement patterns. Dr Pradines explains: "Objects can't lie! We discovered a range of artefacts, for example ceramics, which mean that we can be much more certain that there was active trade between this area and the East. Previously we needed to rely on written accounts - and they are not as reliable. This latest discovery helps us to be much more certain about the exact international trade routes at the time than we could be when relying on manuscripts alone. What struck me most, is the complexity of international trade in the Indian Ocean in the early Middle Ages - an early example of what would now be called globalisation." 

This dig also uncovered two Muslim burial sites from the mid-12th century, showing that the central area of the site was dedicated to ritual activities, probably with a cemetery and a mosque, showing that the local population converted to Islam during or before the 12th century.  
So what is the next chapter for the team? Dr Pradines is optimistic that the site has many more stories to tell. He says; "I would love to find some architectural remains of houses or religious settlements. That will definitely be the next big discovery." 

The excavation, led by Dr Stephane Pradines, was coordinated by the French Department of Cultural Affairs (Réunion) and supported by the ISMC-AKU and Conseil Général (Mayotte). Read more and listen to an interview with Dr Pradines.
